metadata.file_name: 74. Ding et al. (2025). Evaluating test-taking motivation based on process data and its influence on academic performance.pdf
metadata.title: Evaluating test-taking motivation based on process data and its influence on academic performance

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2018 science cognitive item process data for two science clusters (S01 and S02) and restricts the analytic sample to students who completed both clusters and had valid responses for the target items. After excluding 28 students with missing all answers to the target items or with total reaction time outside the normal range (3600 s), the authors analyze 2853 students. For the multilevel regression analyses, they explicitly incorporate the sampling weights provided by the PISA datasets into all multilevel analyses to improve population representativeness. The manuscript does not report replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife), so replicate-weight usage cannot be confirmed; however, complex survey weighting is applied at least at the main estimation stage.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2018 student cognitive items in the science domain, selecting two science clusters (S01 and S02) and excluding adaptive testing items (reading literacy) to maintain consistency. Restricted to representative students from Confucian and Western cultures who completed both S01 and S02. Excluded 28 students who were missing all answers to the target items or whose total reaction time exceeded the normal range (3600 s). For the science academic performance outcome, used the first plausible score (first PV) from the PISA science scaling (with detailed results for all 10 PVs in supplemental materials).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Science (clusters S01 & S02), process data
main_findings.target_variable: Science academic performance (PISA science PV; first plausible score)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Multilevel regression (MLM) with sampling weights. Behavioral effort: Est.=87.338, p<0.001, d=1.083; Self-reported effort: Est.=17.604, p<0.001, d=0.448; Response time effort: Est.=32.449, p<0.001, d=0.773. Additional analysis (Behavioral effort group membership (low vs high)): K-means clustering with Yeo-Johnson transformation; number of clusters selected using elbow rule and silhouette coefficient (final solution: 2 groups). Group sizes: low effort n=1013 (35.5%), high effort n=1840 (64.5%).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Science (clusters S01 & S02) the study leveraged behavioral effort, self-reported effort, and response time effort (RTE) alongside SES and gender in multilevel regression to predict science academic performance (first PV), finding that behavioral effort had the largest positive association (d=1.083). This indicates that process-derived behavioral effort may be a more sensitive indicator of motivation-related performance differences than self-report or response-time effort alone, supporting motivation-aware feedback and interpretation in low-stakes testing.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Science (clusters S01 & S02), process data
main_findings.target_variable: Science academic performance moderation by culture (Western vs Confucian)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Culture interaction moderation in multilevel models: Est.(Behavioral effort×Culture)=-31.565, p<0.05; Est.(Self-reported effort×Culture)=-14.768, p<0.05; Est.(RTE×Culture)=-10.775, p=0.083 (not significant).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Science (clusters S01 & S02) the study leveraged behavioral effort, self-reported effort, and RTE with a culture moderator (Western vs Confucian) in multilevel regression to predict science academic performance, finding that the motivation–performance link was stronger for Western students than for Confucian students for behavioral effort and self-reported effort. This indicates that motivation-based interpretation and interventions may need cultural tailoring, while response-time-effort effects may be less robust to cultural context.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes PISA 2018 science process data from two science clusters (S01 and S02) to develop a situational test-taking motivation construct termed “behavioral effort,” defined by four process indicators: time to last visit, time to first action, number of actions, and user missingness. After excluding 28 students with missing target-item responses or extreme total reaction time (>3600 s), the authors retain 2853 students from China and several Western-culture countries/regions. Behavioral effort is operationalized by K-means clustering into two groups (low effort: n=1013; high effort: n=1840), and its validity is checked against self-reported effort and response time effort (RTE). In multilevel regression with sampling weights, behavioral effort shows the strongest positive association with science performance (Est.=87.338, p<0.001, d=1.083), larger than RTE (d=0.773) and self-report (d=0.448). Cultural moderation is significant for behavioral effort and self-report but not for RTE (p=0.083), and the study uses the first plausible score for the outcome, with full PV results in supplemental materials.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper does not train predictive ML models; instead, it uses K-means clustering to derive behavioral effort groups and then applies multilevel regression (MLM) to test associations with science performance. Therefore, the ML technique fields are intentionally left empty (no supervised ML algorithm is evaluated), even though the study is predictive in the statistical sense (predicting PV-based achievement from motivation indicators).
